title: Just seen Andrei Rublev, my immediate thoughts.

commenti.body: It's been a while since I've watched it, but I remember being deeply moved and while viewing the film, I couldn't help but view the entire movie -- beyond the religious, existential themes -- as a metaphor for the creative process.

To me, it seems odd to say the philosophizing in Stalker and Mirror is not appropriate to the context, because those films in effect establish the context as ideational and philosophical, not a matter of  historical accuracy and realism.

Appropriate or not, I find the philosophizing in those two more compelling than in Rublev, but that is a matter of personal resonance for me.

I think it's ultimately arguing that the creative process is a religious process. In orthodox christianity, the creation of ikons are seen as an opportunity for us as humans to participate in the creation of the universe. Ikons are windows into the divine. In the orthodox view, the ultimate point of human life is "theosis", to become like God, and we can do this by participating in the creative process, in emptying ourselves of our egoic needs and desires and acting out our service, vocation, calling to the world. The artist's way embodies this calling most apparently, as they become creators themselves, but this is the goal for everyone.


Andrei himself goes through several periods of suffering and hardship, each in their own way purifying and emptying him out of all that is blocking his vocation. Similarly, the bellmaker struggles and doubts every step of the way as he guides his town to cast the bell. There's a sense that somehow, our suffering is part of the process, burning away whatever isn't necessary, humbling us in order that we may bring about something pure and holy.


I hope this doesn't all read as though I'm proselytizing, I'm not even Christian myself, I just love the film and just finished reading The Brothers Karamazov so all these ideas are fresh in my mind. For another example of the ikon painting monk character, Rainer Maria Rilke's "Book of Hours" is fantastic and largely centers around similar ideas.

Brilliant! And I remember that the Bellmaker is devasted once he completes the project? Even though he has done a commendable job? I couldn't help but read the sequence in a more meta-manner as a reflection of Tarkovsky's own creative process. In the sense that even though he has created something brilliant, he won't ever be satisfied, even if it is great. I feel like that's a common association with creative types; they set out to create something with the intention that it will fill some existential hole, and yet, there never satisfied.

>Given this same character asks his companion who the Virgin Mary is, and seems dismissive of the core tenets of the religion that surrounds him, it's fair to assume another strong message Tarkovsky laid out here is the idea of people using religion as a veil and nothing more.

It has been while when I saw this film, but this scene has stuck in my mind because of the poignancy.

As I remember it, it goes along the lines of: The Tatar chief, the conqueror of the city, is inside church building accompanied by the traitor, a Russian who collaborated with them. Seeing a fresco of Virgin Mary with child Jesus, the Tatar asks the traitor who is that woman. That is Virgin Mary, the traitor answers. The Tatar lets out a derisive laugh. "What kind of virgin has a child?". The traitor does not answer, but we see his face, he has a peculiar look.

The thing, is the Tatar is almost quoting from the Orthodox liturgy and the tradition of the church. Indeed, what kind of virgin is that, who has child? Barren, yet fruitful. And the traitor - and the Russian spectator - knows those references, and in that moment there is by implication a possibility of grace for the traitor.

That's my interpretation in any case.

It's my favourite Tarkovsky film, and honestly I am not a big fan of his other films but AR is one of my favourite films. Like you said, the dialogue is a lot less preachy and on the nose, he tries less hard to fit in philosophical platitudes and ambiguous symbols and instead focuses on the story development.

A lot of the philosophical platitudes that the characters come out with in Stalker are very vaguely related to the story, and I imagine to OP and definitely to myself it came across as preachy and someone trying too hard to seem profound

I disagree the story and dialogue aren't well connected or aomehow aren't working together.  The rest of what you say is matter of personal resonance like I said, but what you're saying about it and how you are saying it really says more about you than about the film.

Tarkovsky never attempts to "fit in philosophical platitudes and ambiguous symbols."  He says so.  Over and over and over again.  Tarkovsky doesn't do symbols.  He is on record he doesn't want viewers to interpret his movies but just to experience them, e.g.:

>People have often asked me what the Zone [in Stalker] is, and what it symbolises, and have put forward wild conjectures on the subject. I'm reduced to a state of fury and despair by such questions. The Zone doesn't symbolise anything, any more than anything else does in my films: the zone is a zone, it's life, and as he makes his way across it a man may break down or he may come through (Sculpting in Time p.200).

And e.g. during an interview on disc 2 of the Solaris DVD, Mikhail Romadin, art director for Solaris, says:

>On one occasion I overheard a conversation about the 'flying man' in the film Rublev. There was this scene about a man with wings who jumps from a bell tower. Andrei kept asking 'How can we do it so that he doesn't resemble an angel, so that there is no symbolism?' The designers and the cameraman were there and they couldn't think of anything. Somebody said, 'Let's make the wings of wood.' 'No, that wouldn't work either. We need to do something to eliminate the symbolism. Let's make the wings out of feathers.' 'That's another symbol. It'll look like an angel.' And it occurred to me--I said just one word. It should be a sack, a flying sack. Andrei was thrilled, and that's how it was done" (0.02.32-0.03.21).

There are many other such quotes from him and by others who worked with him.

Of course a viewer is free to ignore the known intent of a film maker--that's what I typically do.  But then again, I seldom know what that intent is to begin with.  I am not a mind reader.  So, yes, I thank him for making the movie (with whatever intent he may have had), but once it's out of his hands, what it may or may not mean is out of those same hands and instead in my mind.
